transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
President Trump is facing scathing criticism from California
over remarks he made during a campaign stop in Nebraska.
While talking about the increase in gas prices resulting from the now more than seven-month-old U.S. war with Iran,
the president seemed to suggest that allowing Iran to take out Los Angeles or San Diego
would be a small price to pay compared to the war's eventual benefits.
Steve Futterman has reaction from L.A.
Officials here in California are strongly criticizing the president.
Governor Gavin Newsom on social media called Trump "deranged and dangerous."
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass also had a strong response.
You don't say things like that. You're the president of the United States.
She told NPR "irresponsible" was not a strong enough word to describe the comments.
It's just frightening that a president of the United States would basically call on a foreign power
to attack the nation's second-largest city.
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said his city is not collateral damage and is not expendable.
He told the president to keep San Diego out of his reckless war talk.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman in Los Angeles.
More protests across France today as tens of thousands of demonstrators
called for better conditions in high schools.
Riot police were deployed, numerous arrests reported,
as the demonstrations moved through their second week.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley says students from across the country were out on the streets.
Even students at well-off high schools in big cities like Paris are taking part.
They say out of solidarity with students in the poorer suburbs and rural areas
where schools are more rundown.
The education minister says some of the students' demands are valid.
The far right has called the students hoodlums that burn their schools
and says the problem is a lack of authority.
The far left says police violence is to blame.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reporting.
President Trump now says the United States is willing to help amid fears
of a possible case of mnemonic plague.
One worker at the anti-plague research institute in Siberia died.
There are reports that hundreds of people are being monitored,
and Russian officials have released few details.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this morning during a trip to Iceland
that Russia should share more details.
We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world
so that all of us could react accordingly and appropriately.
But we'll have to make those decisions on the basis of the information
that we're learning and are being provided, and so far that's still quite limited.
The World Health Organization says there's a very low risk to people outside Russia.
The lab employee's death last week has evoked memories of the coronavirus pandemic
and allegations the outbreak originated at a Chinese lab.
The Associated Press cites a WHO spokesperson saying there's currently no indication
of anything similar to the pandemic.
This is NPR.
Grammy-nominated R&B singer Freddie Jackson known for chart-topping hits such as
"You Are My Lady" has died, according to a family statement on his Instagram account today.
Two years ago, Jackson announced he was diagnosed with kidney disease.
Today's Instagram tribute from his family did not disclose a cause of death.
It describes Jackson as a generous soul and a legendary voice
whose songs over the decades became a soundtrack to love stories and celebrations.
Freddie Jackson was 70 years old.
Crime in New York City is at historic lows, according to figures released today.
But reporter Steve Kassenbaum says hate crimes are up as a mayor
faces criticism from Jewish groups over his statements on Israel.
Mayor Zoran Mamdani said a downward trend continues here.
Year to date, murders are down nearly 20 percent.
Officials said shootings reached their lowest level ever
since modern crime statistics have been kept.
But police commissioner Jessica Tisch said hate crimes were up 13 percent year over year.
53 percent of all confirmed hate crimes have targeted Jewish New Yorkers
despite Jews making up only roughly 10 percent of the city's population.
Those numbers are deeply concerning.
The figures come just days after the mayor put an additional $26 million
toward combating anti-Semitism and hate crimes.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Kassenbaum in New York.
This is NPR.

topics.text: President Trump faces criticism from California officials over remarks suggesting Iran attacking Los Angeles or San Diego acceptable during campaign speech
Tens of thousands of protesters across France demonstrate for better high school conditions, police deploy and make arrests during second week
Trump administration offers assistance as Russia reports worker death at Siberia anti-plague research institute, hundreds monitored
Grammy-nominated R&B singer Freddie Jackson, known for hit 'You Are My Lady,' dies at age 70
New York City crime reaches historic lows but hate crimes targeting Jewish residents increase 13 percent year over year
